greeting: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. May the grace and peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who gathers us in His love, be with you all.
penitential:
Lord Jesus, you reveal the depth of your mercy to the contrite heart: Lord, have mercy.
Christ Jesus, you call us to stand in the light of your truth: Christ, have mercy.
Lord Jesus, you promise that your grace is sufficient for us: Lord, have mercy.
psalm_response: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.
homily:
We often think of the great turning points of our lives as grand, public events—the moment a degree is conferred, the day a career begins, the milestone that is marked with a ceremony and a crowd. We are conditioned to measure our lives by the 'firsts' and the 'lasts,' by the visible achievements that we can point to and say, 'This is who I am.' But the Gospel today takes us into a quiet, private room, into the house of a Pharisee, where the most important thing that happens is not a speech or a banquet, but a silent, broken, and beautiful act of love.

There is a woman in this story who has no name, but she has a history. She enters the house of Simon the Pharisee, and she does not ask for permission. She does not wait for an invitation. She carries with her an alabaster flask, and she moves directly to the feet of Jesus. She stands behind him, weeping, and her tears begin to wash his feet. She wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and pours out her costly ointment. It is an act of total vulnerability. It is an act that defies the social order of that room, where people are more concerned with who is 'clean' and who is 'sinner' than they are with the presence of God in their midst.

Think of the stillness of that moment. The clatter of the dishes, the polite conversation of the guests, the judgmental silence of Simon—all of it fades away as this woman pours out her heart. She is not trying to prove anything. She is not trying to justify her past. She is simply present to the only One who can look at her and see not her sins, but her soul. And Jesus, who sees everything, does not pull away. He allows the tears. He receives the ointment. He accepts the devotion of a heart that has finally found its home.

I think of our dear Benjamin today. I think of the way he moved through the world with such a brilliant, curious, and gentle spirit. Ben was a boy who understood, perhaps better than many adults, that life is not about the ledger of what we achieve, but about the quality of the love we offer. He was a boy who loved to build—who spent his hours in GitHub repositories and cloud infrastructure, always trying to understand the architecture of things. He was a boy who dreamed of 'con chim airlines,' a vision of connection and flight that was born from his own bright, imaginative mind. But beneath the logic and the brilliance, there was always that gentle heart. Remember how he offered to give his entire piggy bank to help his uncle? He didn't need to break it, he didn't need to empty it; he simply offered. That was his 'alabaster flask.' It was the offering of a heart that was already tuned to the frequency of the Kingdom.

Alan and Thao, I know the weight you carry. I know that for these past three months, the silence in your home has been a constant companion. You miss the sound of his voice, the way he would greet you in the morning, the way he would giggle when he talked about his dreams. You are living through a season where the world feels as though it has lost its rhythm. You look at the empty space where his laughter used to be, and you wonder how the world can keep spinning when your own world has been so profoundly changed. It is tempting, in the depth of such grief, to look at the ledger of your own life and wonder why the melody of your family changed so abruptly. But look at the woman in the Gospel. She did not have the answers, either. She only had her love. And that love was enough to move the heart of God.

There is a profound, healing truth in what Jesus says to her: 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace.' He does not tell her that her past was easy. He does not tell her that her tears were unnecessary. He tells her that her love, born of faith, has opened the door to a peace that the world cannot give. You are not failing because you are grieving. You are not failing because you miss him. Your tears are like the woman’s tears—they are a testament to the depth of the love you shared. They are the language of a heart that is still, in its own way, washing the feet of the Lord. You are not alone in this. You are a family of four, and that bond is not broken by the distance of heaven. It is only changed. It is being held in the eternity of God, where every tear is gathered and every sorrow is known.

Ryan, my dear brother, you know that heart better than anyone. You stood shoulder to shoulder with Ben—sharing the sunny days on the water, the cozy moments under the blanket, the dreams of the future. When you feel the quiet, remember that your brother is not a ghost. He is a living, radiant presence in the light of the Lord. He is cheering for you with that same bright smile, watching over you, whispering through the quiet moments to keep dreaming, keep being the kind, curious, brilliant soul that you are. You are a brother, and that is a bond that death cannot touch. You are the one who carries his joy forward into the world.

I want to speak to those of you who might be carrying a hidden, heavy stone of self-reproach. Maybe you find yourself replaying the past, wondering if you missed something, if you could have done more, if you should have been more watchful. Please, hear this truth today: God does not send these sorrows as a punishment, and He does not hold you responsible for the mysteries of life that are beyond human control. You were the parents Benjamin needed. You were the family he loved. You did not miss anything. You are not being accused by God, and you must not accuse yourselves. Let that stone fall. You are free to grieve, you are free to miss him, but you are not required to carry the weight of 'what if.' That is a burden that Christ has already taken upon Himself. He is the one who says, 'Your sins are forgiven.' Start by forgiving yourselves. Be as gentle with your own hearts as you were with Benjamin’s.

There is a peace that comes when we stop trying to solve the mystery and start living within it. We are all members of one body. We are all connected by the same Spirit. We are all drinking from the same cup. And in that, we find our strength. Think of the images of him that you hold dear—the sunny day on the yellow boat, the two of you looking out at the airport, the warmth of a winter day shared with family. Those were not just moments; they were glimpses of the Kingdom. They were moments where love was the only thing that mattered. And that love is still real. It is still active. It is still working in the world through the kindness you show to others, through the way you support one another, through the 'Well of Love' that brings clean water to those in need in his name. That is the legacy of a boy who knew that the only way to live is to give.

What do you carry out the door today? It is a small thing, but a real thing. When the weight of the loss feels like it is pressing down on your chest, when the urge to hold onto your grief or your questions feels like a shield, take a breath and remember that you are held by the One who saw the woman’s tears and called them faith. You are loved without limit. When you feel the ache, don't try to solve it. Don't try to fix it. Just whisper his name, and then whisper the name of Jesus. Let those two names be your prayer. You are a family of four, and you are being led, step by step, toward a horizon where there are no more tears, and no more goodbyes. Only the light. Only the love. Only the reunion that is waiting for you at the end of the journey. Keep walking. Keep loving. Keep trusting. You are not alone.
spiritual_communion: My Jesus, I believe that you are present in the Most Holy Sacrament. I love you above all things, and I desire to receive you into my soul. Since I cannot at this moment receive you sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace you as if you were already there and unite myself wholly to you. Never permit me to be separated from you. Amen.
closing: May the Lord bless you and keep you, and may the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and minds today and always.
standing_petitions: For our beloved Benjamin and all who have gone before us, that they may rest forever in the radiant light of Christ.
For all who are grieving, that God may console their hearts, strengthen their hope, and hold them in His everlasting peace.

readings.label: Reading 1
readings.text:
I am reminding you, brothers and sisters,
of the Gospel I preached to you,
which you indeed received and in which you also stand.
Through it you are also being saved,
if you hold fast to the word I preached to you,
unless you believed in vain.
For I handed on to you as of first importance what I also received:
that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures;
that he was buried;
that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures;
that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve.
After that, he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once,
most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep.
After that he appeared to James,
then to all the Apostles.
Last of all, as to one born abnormally,
he appeared to me.
For I am the least of the Apostles,
not fit to be called an Apostle,
because I persecuted the Church of God.
But by the grace of God I am what I am,
and his grace to me has not been ineffective.
Indeed, I have toiled harder than all of them;
not I, however, but the grace of God that is with me.
Therefore, whether it be I or they,
so we preach and so you believed.

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
R. (1) Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.
Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good,
for his mercy endures forever.
Let the house of Israel say,
“His mercy endures forever.”
R. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.
“The right hand of the LORD is exalted;
the right hand of the Lord has struck with power.”
I shall not die, but live,
and declare the works of the LORD.
R. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.
You are my God, and I give thanks to you;
O my God, I extol you.
R. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.

readings.label: Gospel
readings.text:
A certain Pharisee invited Jesus to dine with him,
and he entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table.
Now there was a sinful woman in the city
who learned that he was at table in the house of the Pharisee.
Bringing an alabaster flask of ointment,
she stood behind him at his feet weeping
and began to bathe his feet with her tears.
Then she wiped them with her hair,
kissed them, and anointed them with the ointment.
When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this he said to himself,
“If this man were a prophet,
he would know who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him,
that she is a sinner.”
Jesus said to him in reply,
“Simon, I have something to say to you.”
“Tell me, teacher,” he said.
“Two people were in debt to a certain creditor;
one owed five hundred days’ wages and the other owed fifty.
Since they were unable to repay the debt, he forgave it for both.
Which of them will love him more?”
Simon said in reply,
“The one, I suppose, whose larger debt was forgiven.”
He said to him, “You have judged rightly.”
Then he turned to the woman and said to Simon,
“Do you see this woman?
When I entered your house, you did not give me water for my feet,
but she has bathed them with her tears
and wiped them with her hair.
You did not give me a kiss,
but she has not ceased kissing my feet since the time I entered.
You did not anoint my head with oil,
but she anointed my feet with ointment.
So I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven;
hence, she has shown great love.
But the one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.”
He said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.”
The others at table said to themselves,
“Who is this who even forgives sins?”
But he said to the woman,
“Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

pet_prayers.name: Dad
pet_prayers.text: What happened my son? It's been 3 months since you left us. Missing you so much my whole body aches. Mom cries every day now... What are we going to do now Ben?  Please pray for us.

pet_prayers.text:
Hey Ben,

Rafael Rizzo and his little brother Ben really need your help right now. Please bless them with good health and give them the strength to get through this together. Please watch over Brandon and Flor's health, too.

I miss you a whole bunch. I know you're up in heaven watching over all of us. Whenever you're able to, stop by to visit, yeah? I love you and miss you so much!

Please pray for me and mom to have good health and strength.

Be a guardian angel to Trustin and Ryan as they go through school, and help guide their steps through every year to come.
